findings.title: d1#3's sign-window warning for a payment into Seedelf under a dead register has no test: drop it and the whole Vitest suite passes
findings.scenario: A site asks the wallet to sign a payment into Seedelf Wallet's contract under a register no proof can meet, for example a 47-byte generator or an identity generator. The money is locked for good. The WebAssembly marks that payment seedelf: "dead", and that part is pinned. The window's only words about it are the dapp-seedelf-dead callout (dappUi.warn.deadRegister); otherwise the Pays list just says "Seedelf Wallet's contract". I changed the callout's condition so it never shows, and all 3,548 Vitest tests passed. A refactor that drops or misroutes this warning would ship green, and the user would sign the amount away with no word that nobody can ever spend it. The two sibling callouts in the same block (dapp-seedelf-unsafe for "none", dapp-seedelf-payment for "register") have no test either; those gaps predate this round.
findings.evidence: Copy: git archive of FIXTREE HEAD 10a06db6 plus its wasm/pkg (built 04:06), in ~/.cache/seedelf-review-51/r2tests. The only failures are i18n.test.ts's two machine-draft checks, which also fail on the clean head (23 critical keys still marked machine). grep finds no unit or e2e test that mentions dapp-seedelf-dead or dappUi.warn.deadRegister; the only hit, stake-elsewhere-screens.test.ts, checks TxDetail's tx.out.deadRegister. The WebAssembly half is pinned: Spender::Nobody => "none" at cip30.rs:1303 fails cip30_test a_payment_into_seedelf_says_who_can_take_it.

findings.title: e4a#1's accounts.ts siblings: the merge's and check()'s phrase pins have no test, though the fixer's report says each sibling fails its own case
findings.scenario: Account discovery for phrase A is waiting on Koios for its last probe, the one Koios answers "never used". A Settings "check account N" (accounts.ts:328) can be in the same state. Meanwhile Remove wallet and a restore of phrase B finish. When Koios answers, the pin should end the look as a lock does. Without it, A's found indices are kept into B's known-accounts record, and B's wallet lists and reads accounts its user never added: Koios is asked about B's account-N stake address. I replaced merge's pin with a no-op (E-a4), and separately removed check()'s pin (E-a8). Either one, or both together, passes the whole Vitest suite. accounts-restore-look.test.ts holds the phrase change over the first probe, so the next probe's used() pin throws before merge runs. Nothing changes the phrase during check().
findings.evidence: E-a4: `this.merge(found, pin)` -> `this.merge(found, () => "")` at accounts.ts:278. E-a8: drop `await this.deps.wallet.withKeys(pin);` at :328. Each one gives 24 passed across remove-wallet-reading, accounts-restore-look and remove-wallet (51 passed with accounts.test.ts and accounts-switch-reading added). The full suite with E-a4, E-a8, E-d2 and r2tests#1's mutant applied: 3548 passed; only the 2 i18n checks fail. Control E-a9 (used()'s pin dropped) fails accounts-restore-look: `promise resolved "[ { index: 1, foundAt: 1800000000000 } ]" instead of rejecting`. With used() unpinned, merge's pin never catches it, because phrasePin() pins to whatever phrase it first sees. G6.md says: "each sibling reverted alone fails only its own case; accounts-restore-look.test.ts, remove-wallet.test.ts". That holds for account.ts, pending.ts settleNow and balances.ts (E-a2, E-a3, E-a5 to E-a7 all caught), but not for these two.
findings.fix: Add two accounts-restore-look.test.ts cases. First, hold the probe that Koios answers unused (the index after the last used one) across reset, useFirst, create(B) and recordFirst. Second, hold check(network, n) the same way. Assert each promise rejects with the lock's words and B's list is still [0].

findings.title: r2a#2's error half (failed && !short_whole) is caught by no suite, the ignored parts suite included
findings.scenario: Take a payment whose UTxOs together are short, for example the user's ADA beside a stranger's token piles that cost more than they add. Suppose another order runs into the transaction's size or budget limit. With `failed && !short_whole`, apart refuses with NotEnough, as it did before the fix. Revert that to `failed` and apart returns the size failure instead. In the WebAssembly, build_transfer and withdraw (lib.rs:3209, :3608) fall back to measured_or_more only on build::is_short, and the parts planner (:4106-4271) branches on it too. So a short payment would read as a hard failure there, with a size message (plausible; I didn't build that shape). I reverted only that half (M2b): every non-ignored suite still passes. The search half (M2a) fails apart_test.
findings.evidence: M2b: `Err(match (failed && !short_whole, other, not_enough)` -> `(failed, other, not_enough)`, with short_whole still set. `cargo test -p seedelf-core`, `-p seedelf-wasm` and `-p seedelf-cli` all exit 0. Ignored parts suite in release (`payment_parts_shapes_test -- --ignored`): the head run twice, and M2b once, each gave `0 with problems, 108 refused, 0 of them Max`. Against the head, M2b's 592 lines differ only by 0.01 ₳ on Max lines, and the two head runs differ from each other the same way. Control M2a (the `Grown::Short if whole => { failed = false; break; }` revert at :2860) fails apart_test a_bundle_that_costs_more_than_it_adds_never_stops_what_the_clis_order_pays.
findings.fix: Add an apart_test case: everything together is short, and one order fails by TooLarge or budget (for example, enough token UTxOs sorted first to pass the size limit). Assert build::is_short(&err) and the short words.

findings.title: v3#1's fix (a failed rebuild never reads as ok) has no committed test: drop tally.py's traceless-import rule and nothing notices
findings.scenario: The v3#1 fix makes tally.py and Audit/count.py (hole(), :79/:106) call a module not ok when it rests on a module with no trace. It also makes check.sh's forget() (:215) remove a failed module's build. No test or workflow in the repo runs these scripts, and the verifier's repro wasn't committed. I built a fake package: Lib/A imports Lib/B, A has a trace newer than its source, B has none. The head's tally.py reports "NOT OK Lib.A: rests on Lib.B, which has no trace" and "2 not ok". With that one problem line removed, it reports "1 not ok" and reads A as ok. That is exactly v3#1's failure, and no check would catch it coming back.
findings.evidence: In SCRATCH/r51/work/R2tests/vpkg: Lib/A.lean (`import Lib.B`), Lib/B.lean, and .lake/build/lib/lean/Lib/A.trace = {"log": []}. Ran `python3 -I tally.py Lib` with the head's copy, then with `(f"rests on {under}, which has no trace", under is not None),` removed. Output: `== Lib: 2 modules, 0 Valid, 0 Expected Falsified, 2 not ok` vs `... 1 not ok`. grep finds no test or workflow that names tally.py, count.py or check.sh's forget. I couldn't exercise the Lean-side parts of 40883a55: v4a#1/v4b#1's controls, v5#2's SORRY verdict and the guarded #print axioms.
findings.fix: Add a small `python3 -I` test that builds a fake .lake tree in a temp dir. It should check tally.py and count.py's hole() (traceless import, unreadable trace, sorry line) and check.sh's forget() against a fake failed build log. It runs in milliseconds, with no Lean.

findings.title: New test private-index.test.ts 'is neither the wallet's nor a Seedelf's place' runs 3 to 6.4 s in its own file against Vitest's default 5 s, and times out with nothing wrong
findings.scenario: Run alone, the test takes 0.23 to 0.56 s. After the file's first describe (14 tests), it takes 2.8 to 6.4 s. Neither vite.config.ts nor the test sets a timeout, so Vitest's 5 s applies. On this machine it timed out in 2 of 10 whole-file runs at load 4 to 12, and in 5 of 5 at load about 2. It passed inside the four whole-suite runs. So `npm test` on the branch head can go red with nothing wrong. It also hides what it guards: under the P1, P2, P3 and P5 mutants it failed only by this same timeout. With a 60 s limit it fails P3 and P1 by assertion (`expected { …(13) } to be undefined`).
findings.evidence: `npx vitest run tests/private-index.test.ts --reporter=verbose` at the clean head. At load 4-12: 3283, 2818, 3207, 2964, 3152, 3005, 2935, 2851 ms, plus two runs that hit 5004/5005 ms and timed out. At load 1.6-2.3: 5004, 5004, 5007 ms (all timed out); with -t over the first describe, 5006 ms; with --testTimeout=60000, 6106 ms and (P3) 6402 ms. With -t on this test alone: 561, 533, 571, 324 ms. After just one other test ('reads a restore…' or 'seals nothing…'): 231 and 245 ms. The test's sleep is a no-op (fakes.ts:719), so the time is CPU work that grows with the tests before it. git log -S shows 6aea4fb8 added it.
findings.fix: Give it an explicit timeout, as this round's slow tests already have (`{ timeout: 30_000 }`). Then find what the first 14 tests leave behind that slows its readContractView; the likely suspect is WebAssembly objects that are never freed. Checking the class: no other new test sits near 5 s inside its file.

findings.title: decode_test's big-number test asserts a real-clock bound that adds nothing to the check before it
findings.scenario: a_big_number_past_128_bytes_is_shown_in_hex decodes a 60,000-byte number, asserts the hex text, then asserts `started.elapsed() < 10 s` in a debug build. The equality already proves the hex path; a decimal would differ, and mutant W9 fails at the 129-byte case first. So the clock assertion can only fail on a slow or loaded runner. The work takes milliseconds today, so the risk is small, but it is a real clock by design.
findings.evidence: decode_test.rs:1976-1981 (`let started = std::time::Instant::now(); ... assert!(started.elapsed() < std::time::Duration::from_secs(10), ...)`). W9 (the MOST_DECIMAL_BYTES cut-off disabled) fails at :1963 before reaching the timed part.
findings.fix: Drop the timing assertion, or keep it as an #[ignore] benchmark.
